doc.title: Randy Sandke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997

title: No work from the record, then Concord and Carl Jefferson
summary: The album led to no jobs; he became established as a mainstream player, signed to Concord through Ken Peplowski, and Jefferson accepted his more adventurous records before dying.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: wherever it was, whenever it was reviewed. But it led to absolutely nothing in the way of work. No jobs, no nothing. Couldn’t get into clubs, nobody was hiring me as a sideman, nothing, nothing. So I continued working, getting more and more established in this vein, and also traveling to Europe, getting more established over there everywhere as this mainstream trumpet player. Then by the early 90s — so I’m working with like the younger guys I’m working are some of the guys who are here — Ken Peplowski, Howard Alden, Scott Hamilton, guys who are on Concord. And this was when of course Carl Jefferson was still alive, who is the founder. And largely through Ken I ended up getting on Concord and I still record for them. Now Carl Jefferson, his niche that he found for that record company was to record all this mainstream music which the other labels had totally neglected in this country, and especially the younger guys like Scott Hamilton, Warren Vache and people like that that were out there making a living, getting like the people who listened to them. I mean they really have their fan base — whatever you want to call that constituency. And yet a lot of times they’re really kind of ignored in the larger jazz press or something, and by the record companies. So Carl found that well there’s this audience, there’s this gulf between what this group of the audience wants to hear and what’s being presented and so he was able to do that, and became quite successful. So as I say largely through Ken I was introduced to Carl and I ended up getting signed by Concord. But it was still kind of in the guise of a mainstream artist. And so the records, I’ve just done my fifth. They kind of started out, like my first record with them I just decided well I’m going to make a nice, happy little mainstream jazz record. And one of the problems was that when I was going to the jobs like such as this or the jazz parties, I couldn’t really take that record that I’d done because it alienated people. It still has that effect. I mean I won’t mention any names but there is still a guy who will not hire me because his first experience of listening to me was hearing that record and he can’t reconcile the fact well that — I mean this guy — like I just want to play mainstream or whatever, and I’m afraid he’s going to start playing a Woody Shaw lick or something and ruin the whole —. So I saw that problem and I needed something to sell and to promote for this direction my career was going. So I made this record and just tried to make it as well as I could at the time. And then with each successive one I’ve tried to be a little bit more adventurous, to the third one, which Carl Jefferson was there. And I had him okay Ray Anderson, Mike Brecker, Smitty Smith. And he said fine. And just before we did it he came to New York and we were having dinner the night before we did it and he was saying to me, “you know you can’t be all things to all people. You have to decide what you want to do.” Which was a little deflating to hear just before I’m about to do this record which is really going to be going in another direction, and I’m thinking well he’s going to hear this stuff and he’s going to hate it. So we get into the studio and the first

tune I think we did was that “Lullaby of Broadway.” And surprising enough he liked it, and he heard Ray Anderson and he said, “Wow, this guy’s great.” Which was really nice that I felt like he sort of trusted me and if he heard it and he heard that there was some integrity to it, that he would go along with it. So that was encouraging. Then a short year after that he died. And so now the company is kind of going through a little bit of financial insanity but supposedly everything is going to continue. The last record that I did for them was totally different. Because I’ve been — I kind of found a little more freedom in the writing area, that I’m not so pigeon-holed and I can do more daring things in writing. So the last record that I did was with a symphony orchestra. It’s not out yet, it’ll be out in a couple of months. And I did things on that from contemporary classical music to modern. And even what I got to put on this record is — after my first record, about a year or two later I did a second record, which was kind of going further into more personal areas, different kinds of stuff. And I could not get any record company interested in it. There was just no interest at all. And I invested a lot of money in the project. Finally ten years later some of that is going to be released which is symphony stuff. And I have to admit that’s the stuff that’s closest to my heart because it’s the stuff that is more just me.
